key_insight: Inverse PINNs can recover Manning friction reliably only when shallow-water observations are sufficiently dense, low-noise, and include both depth and velocity; otherwise, identifiability can break down.
engineering_relevance: This benchmark helps engineers judge when PINN-based calibration of hydraulic roughness is trustworthy for flood, river, and channel modeling under sparse monitoring.
method: Two benchmark cases: 1D MacDonald channel with analytical steady solution and 2D sloped channel with parabolic bed from a balanced finite-volume solver.
Train Manning friction as a positive scalar jointly with the flow field using a two-phase PINN strategy: data fit first, then physics residual.
Test sensitivity to observation count, noise level, and observed variable type (depth, velocity, or both).
evidence_signal: In the 2D case, friction errors stayed below 5% with at least 10 depth-velocity observations and noise up to 10% of field standard deviation, but the 1D case showed a persistent ~15% positive bias.
watch_item: Inverse PINN performance can look data-robust while still being structurally unidentifiable, so single-variable observations or very sparse sensors may give misleading friction estimates.
paper_title: How Sparse and How Noisy? Systematic Benchmarking of Inverse Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Manning Friction Estimation in Shallow Water Equations
